column1: Third, monetary policy is represented by a rule for setting the nominal rate of interest. Most central banks today use a short-term nominal interest rate as their instrument for implementing monetary policy. The nominal quantity of money is then endogenously determined to achieve the desired nominal interest rate. Important issues are involved in choosing between money supply policy procedures and interest rate procedures; these are discussed in chapter 11. These three modifications yield a new Keynesian framework that is consistent with optimizing behavior by private agents and incorporates nominal rigidities yet is simple enough to use for exploring a number of policy issues. It can be linked directly to the more traditional aggregate supply-demand (AS-IS-LM) model that long served as one of the workhorses for monetary policy analysis and is still common in most undergraduate texts. Once the basic framework has been developed, section 8.4 considers optimal policy as well as a variety of policy issues.
